meta_desc: Master quadratic equations for JEE Main & Advanced: discriminant, roots, common roots, range and location of roots, plus a free 8-question timed quiz.
excerpt: Quadratics look easy until a JEE Advanced paper hides a common-root or location-of-roots twist inside a two-minute window. Here is the concept map that actually gets tested, how to pace a timed set, the traps that cost marks, and a free 8-question quiz to check yourself.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Most students walk into JEE thinking quadratic equations are the easy marks — factorise, apply the formula, move on. Then the paper hands them something like ‘find the values of a for which both roots of x² − 2ax + a² − 1 = 0 lie between −2 and 4’ and the clock is suddenly the enemy. Quadratic equations for JEE Main and Advanced are rarely about solving one equation. They are about reading which property of the roots a question is really asking for, and answering it without ever finding the roots themselves.

In my experience coaching JEE aspirants, the students who lose marks here are not weak at algebra. They are slow at recognition. They compute a discriminant when the question wanted a range, or hunt for roots when a sum-and-product shortcut was sitting right there. This post maps the exact sub-topics the exam tests, the pacing that keeps a 15-question set under 40 minutes, and the traps that quietly drain marks — then a free timed quiz to pressure-test all of it.

The six concepts JEE actually tests

Every quadratics question on a JEE paper is a disguised version of one of these six ideas. Learn to name the idea in the first ten seconds and half the battle is done.

1. Nature of roots and the discriminant

For ax² + bx + c = 0 with real coefficients, the discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides everything: D > 0 gives two distinct real roots, D = 0 gives equal roots, D < 0 gives a complex conjugate pair. The JEE twist is almost always a parameter. A question like ‘find k so that kx² − 2x + 1 = 0 has equal roots’ is a discriminant problem wearing a costume — and watch the leading coefficient, because if k = 0 the equation is no longer quadratic at all.

2. Sum and product of roots (Vieta)

If α and β are the roots, then α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. This is the single most time-saving tool in the chapter. Almost anything symmetric — α² + β², 1/α + 1/β, α³ + β³ — collapses to an expression in these two quantities. You should never actually solve a quadratic to compute α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ.

3. Common roots

Two quadratics sharing a root is a classic Advanced setup. The clean method: subtract the two equations to eliminate the x² term, which gives a linear equation you solve for the shared root, then substitute back. For a both-roots-common (identical) case, the coefficients are proportional: a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂.

4. Range of a quadratic expression

A quadratic f(x) = ax² + bx + c has a minimum (a > 0) or maximum (a < 0) at x = −b/2a, with value c − b²/4a. Range questions, and ‘for all real x’ inequality questions, both live here. If a paper asks that ax² + bx + c > 0 hold for every real x, you need a > 0 and D < 0 — forgetting the sign of a is the most common single error I see.

5. Location of roots

This is where JEE separates ranks. To force roots to sit relative to a number k, you juggle three conditions together: the sign of D, the sign of a·f(k), and where the vertex −b/2a falls. ‘Both roots greater than k’, ‘k lies between the roots’, ‘exactly one root in (p, q)’ — each has its own combination. Sketching the parabola beats memorising the cases.

6. Quadratic inequalities

To solve x² − 5x + 6 < 0, find the roots (2 and 3), then use the sign of the leading coefficient: an upward parabola is negative between its roots, so the answer is 2 < x < 3. For ‘greater than’ it is the two outer intervals. The wavy-curve (sign scheme) method generalises this to higher-degree factored expressions.

How to pace a timed set

A 15-question quadratics set in 40 minutes gives you a shade under two and a half minutes per question — but you should not spend them evenly. Here is the split that works.

Question typeTarget timeFirst move
Discriminant / nature60–90 sWrite D, check if a can be 0
Symmetric in roots60–90 sApply Vieta, never solve
Common root~2 minSubtract the equations
Range / ‘for all x’~2 minSign of a, then D
Location of roots2–3 minSketch, then D, a·f(k), vertex
Inequality60–90 sRoots, then sign scheme

The discipline that saves the most time is a two-pass strategy: in the first pass, bank every discriminant, Vieta and inequality question. Leave the location-of-roots and multi-condition problems for a second pass, when the easy marks are already secured and your head is clear. Trying to solve them in order is how students run out of time with three gettable questions untouched.

Traps that quietly cost marks

  • Assuming it is quadratic. If the leading coefficient contains a parameter, check the case where it vanishes — the equation may turn linear with a single root.
  • Dropping the sign of a. ‘Expression positive for all x’ needs a > 0 with D < 0. Many candidates write only D < 0.
  • Ignoring ‘distinct’. Distinct real roots means D > 0, strictly. If the question allows equal roots it says so — D ≥ 0 is a different answer.
  • Complex roots and real coefficients. With real coefficients, complex roots come in conjugate pairs. If a problem gives 2 + 3i as one root, − it is telling you 2 − 3i is the other.
  • Forgetting to sketch. Location-of-roots problems solved algebraically without a rough parabola are where sign errors breed.

A worked recognition example

Take ‘if x² + ax + b = 0 and x² + bx + a = 0 (a ≠ b) share a root, find a + b’. Do not solve either. Subtract them: (a − b)x + (b − a) = 0, so x = 1. Put x = 1 into the first equation: 1 + a + b = 0, giving a + b = −1. Fifteen seconds, no formula. That is the recognition speed the exam rewards.

quiz.title: Quadratic Equations JEE Timed Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight JEE-pitched questions on the discriminant, Vieta, common roots, range, location of roots and inequalities. Aim for under 20 minutes, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Quadratic equations for JEE Main & Advanced

questions.q: If α and β are the roots of 2x² − 3x − 5 = 0, what is α² + β²?
For what value of k does kx² − 2x + 1 = 0 have equal roots (k ≠ 0)?
questions.explanation: Equal roots need D = 0: (−2)² − 4(k)(1) = 4 − 4k = 0, so k = 1. Note k = 0 would make it linear, not quadratic.

questions.q: If x² + ax + b = 0 and x² + bx + a = 0 (a ≠ b) share a common root, then a + b equals:
questions.explanation: Subtract the equations: (a − b)x + (b − a) = 0, giving x = 1. Substituting x = 1 into the first: 1 + a + b = 0, so a + b = −1.

questions.q: The minimum value of f(x) = x² − 4x + 7 is:
questions.explanation: For a > 0 the minimum is c − b²/4a = 7 − 16/4 = 3, attained at x = −b/2a = 2.

questions.q: Both roots of x² − 2mx + m² − 1 = 0 lie strictly between −2 and 4 for:
questions.explanation: The equation factors to roots m − 1 and m + 1. Need −2 < m − 1 and m + 1 < 4, giving m > −1 and m < 3, so −1 < m < 3.

questions.q: The solution set of x² − 5x + 6 < 0 is:
questions.explanation: The roots are 2 and 3. An upward parabola is negative between its roots, so 2 < x < 3.

questions.q: x² − 2x + k = 0 has two distinct real roots when:
questions.explanation: Distinct real roots need D > 0: 4 − 4k > 0, so k < 1. (k = 1 gives equal roots, not distinct.)

questions.q: One root of x² + px + 12 = 0 is 4, and x² + px + q = 0 has equal roots. Then q equals:
questions.explanation: Since 4 is a root of the first: 16 + 4p + 12 = 0, so p = −7. Equal roots in the second need p² − 4q = 0: 49 = 4q, so q = 49/4.

faq.q: How important are quadratic equations for JEE Main and Advanced?
faq.a: They are a high-yield topic in their own right and a foundation for complex numbers, coordinate geometry and calculus. Expect one or two direct questions, plus the ideas resurfacing across other chapters — strong quadratics skills quietly lift your whole score.

faq.q: Do I really need to solve the equation to answer most questions?
faq.a: No, and that is the key mindset shift. Sum and product of roots (Vieta), the discriminant, and location-of-roots conditions let you answer most questions without ever finding the roots — which is exactly what saves time under pressure.

faq.q: What is the hardest quadratics sub-topic on JEE?
faq.a: Location of roots. It asks you to combine the sign of the discriminant, the sign of a·f(k), and the position of the vertex all at once. Sketching the parabola for each case is far more reliable than memorising a list of conditions.

faq.q: How should I pace a 15-question quadratics set?
faq.a: Use two passes. First bank the quick discriminant, Vieta and inequality questions in about 90 seconds each; then return to location-of-roots and multi-condition problems with the easy marks already secured. This keeps a 15-question set inside 40 minutes.
